steps.toaLetter.preNoteDeliveryInstructions: Confirm pre-notification information and delivery instructions

stepDescriptions.requestAck.nbRequestReceived: When a {{subType}} document is received, it is indexed and ingested into the system.
stepDescriptions.requestAck.caseProcessing: We create a case in the workflow system so processors can begin work.
stepDescriptions.requestAck.draftContractCreation: For certain contracts, we create a draft contract in the system of record upon receiving a new business request.
stepDescriptions.agentValidation.preValidationRules: To run automated agent validations, we ensure we can verify that the agent's distribution channel, the application signed date, and the agent's credentialing information are complete. If any of these are missing, we can't move forward.
stepDescriptions.agentValidation.agentAppointmentValidati: We check the agent's appointment status to make sure it's active with the appropriate carrier in the appropriate state. (An “active appointment” just means the agent has permission to sell a carrier's products.)
stepDescriptions.agentValidation.agentLOBValidation: We check to make sure the agent is allowed to sell this type of product.
stepDescriptions.agentValidation.agentLicenseValidation: We check to make sure the agent's license is valid in the state where the product listed on the application was sold.
stepDescriptions.agentValidation.agentTrainingValidation: We check product rules for required trainings agents must have to sell the product, and then check to make sure the agent has completed them.
stepDescriptions.agentValidation.agentStatusValidation: Certain carriers do their own agent validations. Once complete, the carrier sends us a confirmation that agent validations were completed on their end.
stepDescriptions.agentValidation.retrieveAgentDetails: We fetch the information from MCS to perform automated agent validations.
stepDescriptions.agentValidation.valiatingAgentDetails: Once we begin running automations, this step will move from not started to in progress. Its completion means all validations are complete.
stepDescriptions.policyValidation.retrieveApplicationData: We fetch the information from the application to perform application validations.
stepDescriptions.policyValidation.valiatingApplicationDet: Once we begin running automations, this step will move from not started to in progress. Its completion means all validations are complete.
stepDescriptions.policyValidation.agentHierarchyValidatio: We confirm the hierarchical relationship between agents on the application so that commission can be applied appropriately.
stepDescriptions.policyValidation.accountValidation: We check product rules for allowable funding sources, and then check the funding source named on the application to make sure it's allowed. Generally, annuities can accept qualified (pre-tax), unqualified (post-tax) funds, or a mix of both, depending on the product.
stepDescriptions.policyValidation.clientInfoValidation: We review the people on the application and their roles to check that the application is complete, containing all required information for the owner, joint owner (if applicable), trust (if applicable) and beneficiaries. We also verify addresses through USPS.
stepDescriptions.policyValidation.premiumAmountValidation: We check that the expected premium listed on the application is within the limits for the product.
stepDescriptions.policyValidation.supportingDocumentValid: We check product rules for required supporting documents, such as disclosures and others required by regulatory authorities. Then we ensure they are enclosed, up-to-date, and complete.
stepDescriptions.policyValidation.signatureValidation: We check product rules for required signatures and verify that the applicable parties (which can include the applicant, co-applicant, trustee, and agent) have signed and dated the application.
stepDescriptions.policyValidation.contractInfoValidation: We check that the product was sold in a state that allows sales of that product.
stepDescriptions.suitabilityReview.suitabilityReview: We check that we've received the complete suitability form.
stepDescriptions.preNotificationLetter.preNoteLetterAckno: If the pre-notification letter was sent by fax and the fax transmission was successful, we receive a confirmation message.
stepDescriptions.preNotificationLetter.cedingCarrierSearc: We look at a database of carrier information to confirm if a ceding carrier will accept the pre-notification letter by fax.
stepDescriptions.preNotificationLetter.cedingCarrierCompa: We look at a database of carrier information to confirm to whom the pre-notification letter must be addressed.
stepDescriptions.preNotificationLetter.carrierDetailValid: We look at a database of carrier information to confirm what delivery method the ceding carrier prefers.
stepDescriptions.preNotificationLetter.preNoteLetterGener: We generate the pre-notification letter, which lets the ceding carrier know that the applicant has requested a transfer, with appropriate applicant and carrier data and letterhead.
stepDescriptions.preNotificationLetter.preNoteLetterProce: We send the pre-notification letter to the ceding carrier by mail or fax, based on their preferences. Once sent, we'll have a tracking number (for mail) or a success message (for fax).
stepDescriptions.toaLetter.toaEligibilityCheck: We check if transfer processing is necessary and can be automated for this carrier and product.
stepDescriptions.toaLetter.presenceOfTransferForm: We look at an industry database to confirm whether the ceding carrier in this case accepts the industry-standard ACORD form, which is what tells us the applicant is requesting money from a product with one carrier (ceding carrier) to be transferred to a product with another carrier. Some carriers require another form to be completed.
stepDescriptions.toaLetter.presenceOfAccordForm: We check that ACORD form (which tells us the applicant is requesting money from a product with one carrier to be transferred to a product with another carrier) is necessary has been received.
stepDescriptions.toaLetter.presenceOfReplacementForm: We check that a replacement form is necessary and has been received.
stepDescriptions.toaLetter.reg60Requirements: We check if regulation 60 paperwork (which determines that the agent who sold the product was acting in best interest of the applicant, according to New York law) is necessary and has been received.
stepDescriptions.toaLetter.loaGeneration: We generate the transfer letter (sometimes called the letter of acceptance, which is a written communication to the ceding carrier that says new carrier can accept the funds) with appropriate applicant and carrier data and letterhead.
stepDescriptions.toaLetter.toaPacketGeneration: We combine transfer letter and necessary supporting documents into a single file so it can be sent over to the ceding carrier.
stepDescriptions.toaLetter.toaPacketDelivery: We send the transfer packet via mail or fax. Once sent, we will have a tracking number (for mail) or a success message (for fax).
stepDescriptions.toaLetter.contractStatusValidation: We confirm in system of record that the contract status is correct.
stepDescriptions.toaLetter.transferPacketDeliveryInstruct: We review the transfer documents and exchange replacement information before creating the transfer packet.
stepDescriptions.toaLetter.createTransferPacket: We combine transfer letter and necessary supporting documents into a single file so it can be sent over to the ceding carrier.
stepDescriptions.toaLetter.sendToaPacket: We send the transfer packet via mail or fax. Once sent, we will receive a tracking number (for mail) or a success message (for fax).
stepDescriptions.toaLetter.preNoteEligibility: We check if a pre-notification letter is needed for this carrier and product
stepDescriptions.toaLetter.preNoteDeliveryInstructions: We verify all information and delivery details for the pre-note letter.
stepDescriptions.toaLetter.preNoteLetterGeneration: We generate the pre-notification letter, which lets the ceding carrier know that the applicant has requested a transfer.
stepDescriptions.toaLetter.sendPreNoteLetter: We send the pre-notification letter to the ceding carrier by mail or fax, based on their preferences.
stepDescriptions.premiumProcessing.erDetailValidation: We create a record in the system of record to record the premium amount and exchange type.
stepDescriptions.premiumProcessing.suspenseValidation: We confirm that funds were received and are held in the suspense account before applying them.
stepDescriptions.premiumProcessing.paymentSourceValidatio: We confirm that the payment source is legitimate and correct.
stepDescriptions.premiumProcessing.agentHierarchyValidati: In order to complete payment processing, we fetch agent hierarchy details so commission can be allocated.
stepDescriptions.premiumProcessing.rateLockEndDateValidat: We check application date to calculate rate lock dates.
stepDescriptions.premiumProcessing.rateLockStartDateValid: We check application date to calculate rate lock dates.
stepDescriptions.premiumProcessing.costBasisValidation: We check the client, request type, and qualification type to determine if application is eligible for cost basis, and verifying the amount, which is important for tax considerations.
stepDescriptions.premiumProcessing.contractInfoValidation: We check that the product was sold in a state that allows sales, that riders selected are allowed for the product, and that selected fund allocations follow product rules.
stepDescriptions.requestCompletion.caseCompleted: The processing work in the workflow system case has been marked complete.
stepDescriptions.requestCompletion.LCContractIssued: We issue the contract once all processing work is complete and premium has processed.
stepDescriptions.requestCompletion.policyPagesIssued: We generate policy pages for the applicant (now owner) of the issued contract.

account.label: account value
account.tooltipBody: This is the amount held within the owner's life insurance policy. The account value accumulates over time as premiums are paid and interest is earned.

fund.label: total fund value
fund.tooltipBody: This is the amount currently invested in funds. It's often the same amount as the account value, but may differ if the owner has any outstanding loans from the policy.
fund.caption: Outstanding Loan: {{ loanValue }}

productType.delayedImmediateFixedAndVariableAnnuity: Delayed Immediate Fixed and Variable Annuity

policyDetails.accountValueTooltip: This is the cash value amount held within the owner's life insurance policy. The account value accumulates over time as premiums are paid and interest is earned.
policyDetails.baseDeathBenefitTooltip: This is the death benefit amount related to the owner's base coverage. It reflects the current figure, so it accounts for any changes to the death benefit that have occurred due to withdrawals or loans. (Note: This figure may differ from total gross death benefit if there are additional lines of coverage or riders that add to the death benefit.)
policyDetails.costBasisTooltip: The cost basis is how much of the account value comes from paid premiums. Account value grows as premiums are paid and earn interest. Withdrawals up to the cost basis amount are tax-free. Owners only pay taxes on gains they withdraw.
policyDetails.goToThisPolicysPage: Go to the {{page}} page for this insurance policy.
policyDetails.netSurrenderValueTooltip: This is how much the owner or their payees can expect if the policy is surrendered. It's the current account value minus surrender charges, outstanding loans, and other fees.

contestability.activeBadgeTooltip: If there’s a death claim during the contestability period, the carrier will take extra care to verify the insured was honest during their application. Carrier may even contest the claim.
contestability.inactiveBadgeTooltip: If there’s a death claim during the contestability period, the carrier will take extra care to verify the insured was honest during their application. Carrier may even contest the claim. This policy’s contestability period ended on contestability end date after contestability period year(s).

coveredParty.riskClassTooltip: Owners are grouped by how risky they are to insure based on health and lifestyle. Less risky=better risk class=lower premium. And vice versa.

policyTimeline.fixedCostPeriodTooltip: During the fixed cost period, there is no cost of insurance charge for this policy. The cost of insurance is exactly what it sounds like: it's how much the carrier charges to cover the risk of insuring a person's life. Ultimately this means that owners of this policy enjoy a lower cost to own and keep their insurance active during the fixed cost period. Once the fixed cost period ends, cost of insurance charges will start.
policyTimeline.maturityDateTooltip: This is the policy's end date. For cash value policies, the maturity date is often set to when the person reaches a certain age (say, 95 or 100). If the owner outlives the policy, they get the cash value (minus charges) at maturity.
policyTimeline.policyLengthTooltip: Policy length is just what it sounds like: it's how long the policy lasts. Some policies have a set term (shown in number of years) and end date, while others last until death of the insured.

productDetails.productNameTooltip: This is the product name that you’ll see referenced in internal documentation. It’s different from the product marketing name that’s used in correspondence and will be familiar to the owner.

baseCoverage.sideSheetBody: Coverage changes can impact the policy beyond changing the death benefit. Any change resets the seven year period used for the 7-pay premium test; decreases can impact other guidelines tests. If a policy fails any of these tests, the policy loses important tax advantages.
baseCoverage.footer: *Never seen these before? These fields reflect rules that are specific to Every Life's Universal Life product.
baseCoverage.baseDeathBenefitPopover: This is the death benefit amount related to the owner's base coverage. It reflects the current figure, so it accounts for any changes to the death benefit that have occurred due to withdrawals or loans. (Note: This figure may differ from total gross death benefit if there are additional lines of coverage or riders that add to the death benefit.)
baseCoverage.originalDeathBenefitPopover: When the owner first bought their policy, they were insured for this amount. Owners may increase or decrease coverage over time (according to certain policy rules). See base death benefit and total gross death benefit to understand their current coverage.

additionalInformation.netAmountRisk: Net amount at risk for policy
additionalInformation.netAmountRiskPopover: This factor helps the insurance company understand how much money is at risk if the insured on the policy died today. This is used for finance and accounting purposes.

documents.actionsTooltip: For now, some file types (e.g. CTX and DOC) are download only. We are currently  working on making all inbound file types viewable within Zinnia Live. Stay tuned!
documents.documentIdentifierTooltip: This is a unique set of characters assigned to each document and tells you a bit about the document itself. If the document identifier is a single string of characters, you’ll know it’s an outbound document. If it has 3 sections separated by hyphens, it’s an inbound document. For inbound documents, the first set of characters is the date it was received in YYYYMMDD format. The second set is how it was received (e.g., DS = Docusign, EM = Email, F = Fax, M = EApp, 1-8 = Mailroom scan, etc.). And the final set is the unique id.
documents.linkedTo: This document is linked to this {{type}}.
documents.noResults: Looks like there aren't any documents to display.

matchCard.currentValuePopover: This is the total amount the carrier has contributed to the match account. After the match vesting period ends, this accrued amount will be added to the account value.
matchCard.label: Match
matchCard.matchRatePopover: For every dollar contributed by the policy owner, the carrier will contribute a match amount at this percentage.
matchCard.maxLifetimeMatchPopover: This is the maximum amount the carrier will contribute to the match fund over the life of the policy.
matchCard.vestingPeriodPopover:
This is the amount of time before the carrier will add the accrued match amount to the account value. If the owner surrenders the policy before the vesting period ends, the carrier keeps the current value of the match account.
All the money in match could be forfeited if you end the policy before this period ends.

fundDetails.electedFundsTooltip: Elected funds are those currently selected by the owner to receive money from the holding fund. Each of the funds below will receive a deposit from the holding fund(s) on the next sweep date. The amount each will get is determined by the owner's selected allocations.
fundDetails.holdingFundsTooltip: Holding funds are where deposits first land. When the owner pays premium into the policy, cost of insurance and any other fees come out first. Then the rest is held in the holding fund(s) for a period of time before being "swept" or moved into elected funds, according to the owner's selected allocations.
fundDetails.notElectedFundsTooltip: Not elected funds are not currently selected by the owner to receive money. However, these funds may have been selected for a time in the past and so may hold value that is contributing to the total account value.
fundDetails.title: Details

fundsTable.fundValueTooltip: This is the amount currently invested in funds. It's often the same amount as the account value, but may differ if the owner has any outstanding loans from the policy.
fundsTable.interestRateTooltip: This is the rate of growth being earned on the amount invested within a fixed fund.
fundsTable.nextSweepDateTooltip: On this date, all money in the holding fund will be "swept" or moved into the policy's various funds, according to the owner's selected fund allocations. In most cases, the sweep date happens on the same date every month.

segmentsTable.segmentIDTooltip: This a unique numeric identifier for each segment. Segment IDs start with 1 for the first-ever segment and count up from there. Policies with segment IDs in the hundreds are older policies. At most, there will be 13 segments open at a time, which you’ll see in this table.
segmentsTable.startDateTooltip: This is the date the segment opens, and the index period begins. The index period is a set time during which the money within the segment can earn interest based on the rules of the fund. The start date is always the day that money was “swept” or moved into the segment.
segmentsTable.endDateTooltip: This is the date the segment closes, and the index period ends. The index period is a set time during which the money within the segment can earn interest based on the rules of the fund. In most cases, the end date is 12 months from the start date.
segmentsTable.depositAmountTooltip: This is the amount that was deposited into the fund. It’s the amount of premium paid into the policy minus any applicable charges, including cost of insurance and fees.
segmentsTable.segmentCapTooltip: This is the rate ceiling of what this fund can earn. Each of the funds in the policy will follow a certain stock market index (like S&P 500 or Dow Jones Average) during the segment’s index period. The money in the segment can earn interest based on the performance of this tracked index fund during this time, but earnings can be limited by a segment cap. For example, even the supporting index grows a lot, the earnings can not exceed the segment cap rate.
segmentsTable.participationRateTooltip: This is the rate ceiling of what this fund can earn. Each of the funds in the policy will follow a certain stock market index (like S&P or Dow Jones Average) during the segment’s index period. The money in the segment can earn interest based on the performance of this tracked index fund during this time, but earnings can be limited by a participation rate. For example, if the participation cap is 80% and the tracked index fund increases by 15% during the segment period, the interest credit will be limited to 80% of the 15% gain, so the money will only earn 12% (80% × 15% = 12%).

features.activeTooltip: Active riders or features are those that are on the policy and are being used currently. That means the insured has submitted a claim for related benefits.
features.availableTooltip: Available riders or features are those that are currently on the policy. The owner is paying for these additional types of coverage and may submit a claim related to it.
features.notElectedTooltip: Not elected riders or features are those that the owner has the option to add to this policy. They are not currently paying for these additional types of coverage and may not currently submit claims for related benefits. But they could potentially add these to the policy.
features.terminatedTooltip: Terminated riders or features are those that are either expired or cannot be used again.

riders.activeTooltip: Active riders or features are those that are on the policy and are being used currently. That means the insured has submitted a claim for related benefits.
riders.availableTooltip: Available riders or features are those that are currently on the policy. The owner is paying for these additional types of coverage and may submit a claim related to it.
riders.chronicIllnessBenefit: Up to {{percent}}% of death benefit paid over a maximum of {{period}} payments
riders.criticalIllnessBenefit1: For tier 1 illnesses: {{t1Percent}}% of the death benefit or ({{t1Amount}}), whichever is less.
riders.criticalIllnessBenefit2: For tier 2 illnesses: {{t2Percent}}% of the death benefit or ({{t2Amount}}), whichever is less.
riders.notElectedTooltip: Not elected riders or features are those that the owner has the option to add to this policy. They are not currently paying for these additional types of coverage and may not currently submit claims for related benefits. But they could potentially add these to the policy.
riders.terminatedTooltip: Terminated riders or features are those that are either expired or cannot be used again.

sidesheet.newAppliedAmountTooltip: This is how much money was added to the account value after a reversal of a premium
sidesheet.appliedAmountTooltip: This is how much money was added to the account value after processing. Applied amount is usually the same as the submitted amount. But it can differ if the submitted amount broke the policy test limits, which can cause some funds to be returned (called a “force out.”)
sidesheet.processDateTooltip: This is the date when the transaction went through processing. It tells you when the transaction was included in the batch cycle. Process date may differ from the effective date (the date the transaction is actually applied to the policy).
sidesheet.submittedAmountTooltip: This is how much was submitted. In other words, the owner wrote a check or initiated a funds transfer for this amount. Submitted amount may differ from the applied amount if we could only apply a lower amount due to policy test limits. These are legal limits to how much an owner can pay into the policy within a certain time period. This can cause some funds to be returned to the owner (called a “force out”).
sidesheet.reverseRecreateSubmittedAmountTooltip: This is how much was sent for payment initially. The owner wrote a check or initiated a funds transfer for this amount, and the request to apply this amount was submitted in our system. Submitted amount may differ from the applied amount if we could only apply a lower amount due to policy test limits. These are legal limits to how much an owner can pay into the policy within a certain time period. This can cause some funds to be returned to the owner (called a “force out”).
sidesheet.lapseProcessDateTooltip: This is the date when the transaction went through processing. It tells you when the transaction was included in the batch cycle. Process date may differ from the effective date (the date the transaction is actually applied to the policy).
sidesheet.lapseDateTooltip: This is the date when the policy lapsed. The owner didn’t make a grace payment, so now the policy is officially inactive.
sidesheet.lapseGracePeriodTooltip: These dates tell you how long the owner has to make the required grace payment to keep the policy active. The first date is when the policy went into pending lapse status, and the second is the deadline to make the required grace payment.
sidesheet.lapseGracePeriodMinPaymentTooltip: This is the minimum amount the owner must pay in premium before the grace period ends to keep their policy active (and their coverage and account value intact).
sidesheet.lapseReinstatementPeriodTooltip: This tells you how much time following lapse date the owner has to begin the process to reinstate the policy.

withdrawalSidesheet.requestedWithdrawalAmountTooltip: This is how much the owner is requesting to withdraw from the account value. This number can differ from the actual total payment or the actual withdrawal amount depending on the disbursement type (gross or net) selected and the policy’s rules around withdrawal fees.
withdrawalSidesheet.totalPaymentTooltip: This is how much will actually be paid from this withdrawal. It's the requested amount minus any applicable transaction fees.
withdrawalSidesheet.actualWithdrawalAmountTooltip: This is how much will actually be withdrawn from the account value. If the owner selected net disbursement, we will withdraw any transaction fees (if applicable) in addition to the requested withdrawal amount. If gross was selected, the actual and requested withdrawal amounts will match.
withdrawalSidesheet.effectiveDateTooltip: This is the date used to calculate all the available account values for this withdrawal. Because funds in the account value are invested, the account value can change day by day. Processing can happen at any time, so we need to know at what point  to effectively withdraw the funds, even if we’re processing the transaction some days before or after.
withdrawalSidesheet.processDateTooltip: This is the date when the transaction went through processing. It tells you when the transaction was included in the batch cycle. Process date may differ from the effective date (the date the transaction is actually applied to the policy).
withdrawalSidesheet.fundDisbursementTypeTooltip: The account value is invested in one or more investment funds. When we withdraw the money, we need to know how to take the amount from each investment fund.  Pro rata means take an equal amount from each investment fund. Custom allows the owner to choose a certain amount from each investment fund.
withdrawalSidesheet.disbursementTypeTooltip: Disbursement type affects how fees are paid. Gross means the fees are subtracted from the requested amount; net means they are added. Not all policies have fees so depending on the carrier and the product, this selection may not make a meaningful difference.
withdrawalSidesheet.federalTaxTooltip: Withdrawals in amounts greater than what the owner has paid in premiums are taxable. We can “withhold” the federal tax, meaning we can pay a certain amount to the IRS on behalf of the owner from the amount they withdraw. Or the owner can decide to pay the taxes themselves later.
withdrawalSidesheet.stateTaxTooltip: Withdrawals in amounts greater than what the owner has paid in premiums are taxable. We can “withhold” the state tax, if applicable, meaning we can pay a certain amount to the  state tax authority on behalf of the owner from the amount they withdraw. Or the owner can decide to pay the taxes themselves later.

newLoanSideSheet.title: Loan
newLoanSideSheet.processedAmountTooltip: This is the amount that was actually deducted and set aside for the loan. Usually the processed amount and loan amount match. But it can vary from the loan amount if net disbursement type was selected during loan processing, and the carrier charges fees for loans for this product.
newLoanSideSheet.loanInterestRateTooltip: This is the rate at which interest accrues annually. A loan from a cash value life insurance policy is a loan from the insurance carrier with the account value on the policy used as collateral. When an owner borrows from their account value, the loan principal will accrue interest at an annual percentage rate. The total accrued for the year is then applied to the principal on the interest date. The interest accrued must be paid back to close the loan . Many owners choose to leave loans open indefinitely, and accept the risk of a lower death benefit.
newLoanSideSheet.loanInterestRateTypeTooltip: This describes whether the interest rate on the loan can change over time or not. Fixed interest rates don’t change, while variable, indexed, and adjustable interest rates may change over time.
newLoanSideSheet.effectiveDateTooltip: This is the date used to calculate all the available account values for this loan. Because funds in the account value are invested, the account value can change day by day. Processing can happen at any time, so we need to know at what point to effectively withdraw the funds, even if we're processing the transaction some days before or after.
newLoanSideSheet.processDateTooltip: This is the date when the transaction went through processing. It tells you when the transaction was included in the batch cycle. Process date may differ from the effective date (the date the transaction is actually applied to the policy).
newLoanSideSheet.fundDisbursementTypeTooltip: The account value is invested in one or more investment funds. When we withdraw the money, we need to know how to take the amount from each investment fund. Pro rata means take an equal amount from each investment fund.Custom allows the owner to choose a certain amount from each investment fund.

header.eligiblePopover: The owner can take a loan from the account value on this policy. Owners can borrow at any time, as long as the funds are available. A loan can reduce the death benefit unless and until it is paid back.
header.ineligiblePopover: This policy doesn't have enough account value for a loan. Owners can borrow from their policy at any time, as long as the funds are available.

loanRules.headline: Loan Rules
loanRules.loanInterestMethodTooltip: This tells you how the loan’s interest is applied. Arrears means the interest is charged at the end of the policy year. This means a payment that occurs mid-year can reduce the daily interest amount and thus, the interest owed at the end of the year. Advance means the insurance carrier charges annual interest for the loan up front on the day the loan starts. So if the loan is taken halfway through the policy year, interest for the remaining half the year is charged when the loan starts. If loan repayment occurs within a policy year, there’s typically no refund for the interest paid in advance.

outstandingLoans.headline: Outstanding Loans
outstandingLoans.inactiveCard: There are no outstanding loans on this policy.
outstandingLoans.interestRateTooltip: This is the rate at which interest accrues annually. A loan from a cash value life insurance policy is a loan from the insurance carrier with the account value on the policy used as collateral. When an owner borrows from their account value, the loan principal will accrue interest at an annual percentage rate. The total accrued for the year is then applied to the principal on the interest date. The interest accrued must be paid back to close the loan . Many owners choose to leave loans open indefinitely, and accept the risk of a lower death benefit.

additionalInformation.creditRateTooltip: This is how much the loan principal is still earning in interest gains. (Yes, earning!) A loan from a cash value life insurance policy is a loan from the insurance carrier with the account value on the policy used as collateral. When an owner borrows from their policy, the principal loan amount is kept separate but remains invested and continues to earn  gains at an annual percentage rate, which is shown here as a credit rate. The credit earned on the loan amount doesn’t need to be paid back.
additionalInformation.loanCollateralTooltip: This is the loan principal, plus any credit earned since the loan started. This amount is held separate from the unloaned portion of the account value and has its own credit rate at which it gains earnings. A loan from a cash value life insurance policy is a loan from the insurance carrier with the account value on the policy used as collateral. When an owner borrows from their policy, the principal loan amount remains invested and continues to earn interest gains at an annual percentage rate.
additionalInformation.loanPrincipalTooltip: The total shown here is what was borrowed, plus any interest accrued. A loan's principal is the original amount borrowed. Interest charges accrues annually, and outstanding interest is added to remaining principal, according to the interest method.
additionalInformation.loanRepaymentTypeTooltip: Loans can be repaid as interest first or principal first. Interest first means that before any payment amount is applied to the principal  balance the interest will be paid first. Principal first means the opposite: payment will first be applied to the principal balance before interest is paid down.

popOver.grossDeathBenefit: This is what the policy pays out when the insured dies. It’s usually the same as the base death benefit (also known as the face amount) but it can include additions (like returned premiums) in some cases.
popOver.netDeathBenefit: This is roughly how much the beneficiaries will receive from a death claim. The amount reflects the total gross death benefit minus outstanding loans. It doesn't include interest charges that can only be calculated at the time a death claim processes. Consider it a helpful, but inexact amount.
popOver.deathBenefitOption: Some policies come with an option to increase coverage over time. Level death benefit stays the same for the life of the policy. An increasing death benefit goes up as the policy's account value increases.

popOver.costBasis: The cost basis is how much of the account value comes from paid premiums. Account value grows as premiums are paid and earn interest. Withdrawals up to the cost basis amount are tax-free; owners only pay taxes on interest gains. (Note: Cost basis can differ from the all-time premium amount if the owner has made withdrawals.)
popOver.gracePeriodBeforeLapse: These dates tell you how long the owner has to make the required grace payment to keep the policy active. The first date is when the policy went into pending lapse status, and the second is the deadline to make the required grace payment.
popOver.gracePeriodMinPayment: This is the minimum amount the owner must pay in premium before the grace period ends to keep their policy active (and their coverage and account value intact.)

fields.eligibleForLoanPopover: This amount is how much the owner may borrow from the account value of their policy. Loans have consequences. Aside from incurring interest, a loan may reduce the owner’s death benefit.
fields.estimatedNetDeathBenefitPopover: This is roughly how much the beneficiaries will receive from a death claim. The amount reflects the total gross death benefit minus outstanding loans. It doesn't include interest charges that can only be calculated at the time a death claim processes. Consider it a helpful, but inexact amount.
fields.availableLoanInterestRatePopover: If the owner wants to take a loan, this is the interest rate they'll be offered. Loans from a cash value life insurance policy accrue interest at a certain percentage rate. Interest will be applied to the principal annually. Interest must be paid back along with principal in order to close the loan and restore the death benefit.
fields.availableLoanCreditRatePopover: If the owner wants to take a loan, this is the credit rate they'll earn. (Yes, earn!) A loan from a cash value life insurance policy is a loan from the insurance carrier with the account value on the policy used as collateral. When an owner borrows from their policy, the principal loan amount is kept separate but remains invested and continues to earn gains at an annual percentage rate.

policyTestsCard.title: Policy Tests
policyTestsCard.statusToolTipMecYes: This policy is a modified endowment contract (MEC). A MEC is a life insurance policy that has lost tax advantages because it contains too much cash value. A policy becomes a MEC when the owner pays too much premium in too short of a period to pass the 7-pay premium test.
policyTestsCard.statusToolTipMecNo: This policy is not a MEC, which stands for modified endowment contract. A policy becomes a MEC when the owner pays too much premium in too short of a period to pass the 7-pay premium test. A MEC doesn't have the same tax advantages as a cash value life insurance policy.
policyTestsCard.statusToolTipDate: This policy was last tested for MEC status on {{mecTestDate}}.

amountRemaining.label: Amount remaining until current guideline limit
amountRemaining.tooltipBody: This is how much the owner could pay in premium before reaching the currently applicable guideline limit. This limit is defined by the Guideline Premium Test, which is a legal requirement for determining if a policy "meets the definition of life insurance." If the owner pays more than the amount here, the carrier will return the overage amount paid.

basis.label: Guideline basis
basis.tooltipBody: This is how much the owner has paid in premiums (minus any withdrawals) so far during the life of the policy. It’s the amount that’s counting against the policy’s current guideline premium limit. By law, carriers must use the guideline premium test to determine if the policy meets the definition of life insurance. To do so, the sum of all premiums paid minus withdrawals cannot exceed the currently applicable guideline limit.

total.label: Total current guideline limit
total.tooltipBody: This is the currently applicable guideline limit amount. The owner cannot pay more than this amount in premium right now. The amount shown here is whichever is the greater of: the guideline single premium or the sum of guideline level premiums since issue. These limits are determined by law that governs the definition of life insurance. If the owner pays beyond the relevant limit at any time, the carrier will return the overage amount paid. This is often referred to as a "force out".

sevenPay.amountExcessMecTooltip: This is how much premium was applied beyond the policy’s 7-pay limit. This overage amount makes the policy a modified endowment contract (MEC), which is a specific type of life insurance contract with fewer tax advantages. Once a policy becomes a MEC, the change cannot be reverted.
sevenPay.amountRemainingTooltip: This is how much the owner could pay in premium right now without the policy becoming a modified endowment contract (MEC). Most owners do not want their policy to become a MEC because that means they lose important tax advantages of owning a cash value policy. Once the 7-year period is over for the policy’s 7-pay premium test, the owner won’t have to worry about this limit unless there is a material change. A material change, like a coverage increase, can reactivate the 7-pay test for another 7 years.
sevenPay.annualPremiumTooltip: This is the annual amount for this policy set by law. The formula carriers must use to do the 7-pay premium test is (annual 7-pay premium x year in 7-year period) + any rollover amount from the year before. (This is calculated for you in current 7-pay premium limit.)
sevenPay.basisTooltip: This is how much the owner has paid in premiums (minus any withdrawals) during the active 7-pay premium test window. By law, carriers must use the 7-pay premium test to determine MEC status. To prevent the policy from becoming a MEC, the sum of all premiums paid minus any withdrawals during an active 7-pay period cannot exceed the current 7-pay premium limit. The 7-pay premium basis reflects the amount currently being counted against the 7-pay premium limit.
sevenPay.inactiveEndText: . It may restart for another 7-year window if a material change occurs.
sevenPay.inactiveStartText: This policy’s 7-pay premium test period ended
sevenPay.isMecTooltip: This policy is a modified endowment contract (MEC). A MEC is a life insurance policy that has lost tax advantages because it contains too much cash value. A policy becomes a MEC when the owner pays too much premium in too short of a period to pass the 7-pay premium test.
sevenPay.isNotMecTooltip: This policy is not a MEC, which stands for modified endowment contract. A policy becomes a MEC when the owner pays too much premium in too short of a period to pass the 7-pay premium test. A MEC doesn't have the same tax advantages as a cash value life insurance policy. This policy was last tested for MEC status on {{ mecTestDate }}.
sevenPay.testPeriodTooltip: These are the start and end dates for the active 7-pay premium test period. During this time, there are certain limits to how much an owner can pay in premium before the policy becomes a modified endowment contract (MEC). To prevent becoming MEC, the sum of the premiums minus withdrawals in the initial seven years after issue or a subsequent material change cannot exceed the sum of the annual 7-pay premium limit for those seven years.
sevenPay.title: 7-pay premium test
sevenPay.totalLimitTooltip: This is the maximum amount the owner can pay in premium this year without the policy becoming a MEC. It reflects the formula carriers must use to do the 7-pay premium test: (Annual 7-pay premium limit x year in 7-year period) + any rollover amount from the year before. Once the 7-year period is over for the policy’s 7-pay premium test, the owner won’t have to worry about this limit unless there is a material change (like a coverage increase) that reactivates the 7-pay test for another 7-year period.

amount.assistiveText: A full withdrawal will end the owner's coverage.
amount.disbursementTypeTooltip: Disbursement type affects how fees are paid. Gross means the fees are subtracted from the requested amount; net means they are added. Not all policies have fees so depending on the carrier and the product, this selection may not make a meaningful difference.
amount.effectiveDateTooltip: This is the date used to calculate all the available account values for this withdrawal. Because funds in the account value are invested, the account value can change day by day. Processing can happen at any time, so we need to know at what point to effectively withdraw the funds, even if we're processing the transaction some days before or after.
amount.fundDisbursementTypeLabel: How will this amount be taken from funds?
amount.fundDisbursementTypeTooltip: The account value is invested in one or more investment funds. When we withdraw the money, we need to know how to take the amount from each investment fund. Pro rata means take an equal amount from each investment fund. Custom allows the owner to choose a certain amount from each investment fund.

taxes.federalTooltip: Withdrawals in amounts greater than what the owner has paid in premiums are taxable. We can "withhold" the federal tax, meaning we can pay a certain amount to the IRS on behalf of the owner from the amount they withdraw. Or the owner can decide to pay the taxes themselves later.
taxes.label: Taxes
taxes.stateTooltip: Withdrawals in amounts greater than what the owner has paid in premiums are taxable. We can "withhold" the state tax, if applicable, meaning we can pay a certain amount to the state tax authority on behalf of the owner from the amount they withdraw. Or the owner can decide to pay the taxes themselves later.
taxes.title: How much should we withhold for taxes?

summary.actualWithdrawalAmountTooltip: This is how much will actually be withdrawn from the account value. The owner selected net disbursement, so we will withdraw any transaction fees (if applicable) in addition to the requested withdrawal amount.
summary.effectiveDateTooltip: This is the date used to calculate all the available account values for this withdrawal. Because funds in the account value are invested, the account value can change day by day. Processing can happen at any time, so we need to know at what point to effectively withdraw the funds, even if we're processing the transaction some days before or after.
summary.federalTaxesTooltip: Withdrawals in amounts greater than what the owner has paid in premiums are taxable. summary.fundDisbursementTypeTooltip: The account value is invested in one or more investment funds. When we withdraw the money, we need to know how to take the amount from each investment fund. summary.requestedWithdrawalTooltip: This is how much the owner is requesting to withdraw from the account value. This number can differ from the actual total payment or the actual withdrawal amount depending on the disbursement type (gross or net) selected and the policy’s rules around withdrawal fees.
summary.stateTaxesTooltip: Withdrawals in amounts greater than what the owner has paid in premiums are taxable. We can "withhold" the state tax, if applicable, meaning we can pay a certain amount to the state tax authority on behalf of the owner from the amount they withdraw. Or the owner can decide to pay the taxes themselves later.

rmd.title: Required Minimum Distribution
rmd.totalRMDAmountTooltip: This is the total amount of the RMD that the owner is required to distribute. It's the requested amount minus any applicable transaction fees.
rmd.remainingRMDAmountTooltip: This is the amount of the RMD that the owner is still required to distribute.
rmd.calculationDateTooltip: This is the date on which the RMD is calculated.
rmd.calculationTypeTooltip: This is the method used to calculate the RMD.

rules.title: Withdrawal Rules
rules.minWithdrawalTooltip: To make a withdrawal, the owner must request at least this amount.
rules.maxWithdrawalTooltip: This is the maximum amount the owner can withdraw while still keeping their policy active.
rules.maxAnnualFuture: {{maxDuring}} per year through {{date}}, then {{maxAfter}} per year
rules.maxAnnualTooltip: This is how many times an owner can make a withdrawal (of any eligible amount) within a policy year.
rules.coverageLimitTooltip: Owners can withdraw this amount without impacting their coverage. In other words, they can withdraw this amount and still keep their death benefit intact.

withdrawals.allTimeWithdrawalsTooltip: This is how much the owner has withdrawn from the account value since they've owned their policy.
withdrawals.annualWithdrawalsRemainingTooltip: This is the number of withdrawals remaining for the policy year.
withdrawals.eligibleForWithdrawalTooltip: Withdrawals from the account value are allowed right now. Withdrawals may reduce the death benefit.
withdrawals.netSurrenderValueTooltip: This is how much the owner or their payees can expect if the policy is surrendered. It's the current account value minus surrender charges, outstanding loans, and other fees.
